title: Unit ECon Practical Playbook for Field Engineers
content:
Purpose
This is a compact, field-friendly playbook for sales engineers, solutions folks, and partners who need to: 1) make tight, credible latency/cost claims at pre-sales and demo, 2) show concrete proof points (quick experiments or tabletop math), and 3) anticipate competitor pushback with crisp rebuttals. The voice should be pragmatic — short scripts, repeatable demos, and simple formulas that map to real numbers.

Context and positioning thesis (one-liner)
Redwood converts latency predictability into unit-dollar savings: fewer model fallbacks, better batch amortization, and smaller worker pools for the same throughput. We sell predictable ms and $/1k-tokens as operational levers, not abstract performance bragging.

Core claims (audience: engineering buyer / platform lead)
- Predictable tail-latency: p95/p99 that align with customer SLOs — demonstrable via a 10-minute synthetic run.
- Lower per-token operational cost at scale through batching + prefix/KV caching: typical reduction 25–45% depending on session length and cache hit rate.
- Graceful degradation: automated fallback to smaller quantized variants that preserve availability instead of queueing.

Field proof patterns (fast experiments you can run in a call or short POC)
1) The 10-minute p95 check (credibility > speed):
   - Setup: 2 concurrent clients, 8 tokens avg request length, 200ms think time between requests -> target 50 RPS.
   - Measure: p50/p95/p99 for 10 minutes on customer model vs redwood-hosted equivalent.
   - Outcome to show: ‘we're within N ms of your baseline but at X% lower cost per token after batching’ (export CSV + screenshot).
2) The session amortization demo (shows value of caching):
   - Use a stateful chat flow with repeated context (~100 tokens) over 30 messages.
   - Show token delta and cost delta with prefix caching ON vs OFF. Highlight percent savings and latency gain on subsequent messages.
3) The scale-sweep (throughput economics):
   - Run incremental RPS from 10 -> 100 -> 1k (short bursts). Show how Redwood autoscaling + burst smoothing keeps p95 stable while competitor p95 balloons.

Simple formulas (quick math to bring to the whiteboard)
- Effective cost per request = (tokens_per_request * $/token) * (1 - cache_hit_rate) + overhead_per_request
- Amortized GPU cost per 1M tokens = (hourly_gpu_cost * hours_per_month) / (monthly_tokens_served) -> translate to $/1k tokens
- Batch savings (approx) = 1 - (avg_batch_size_with_rb / avg_batch_size_competitor) * kernel_efficiency_factor
Note: have a back-of-envelope Google Sheet ready with sliders for tokens, RPS, cache hit %, batch size.

Competitive notes & rebuttals (short, battle-tested)
- Competitor: “We are faster at short requests”
  Rebuttal: For short single-turn requests, raw ms matters — run the 10-minute p95 check and show tail behavior. For multi-turn or high-throughput apps, our batching + cache amortization typically tips the unit economics in our favor.
- Competitor: “We have cheaper GPUs / fixed pricing”
  Rebuttal: Fixed pricing hides unit variability and slow tail behavior. Ask for their p95 at target RPS and show how unpredictable tail events can cause substantially higher apparent cost (queueing, retries, failed fallbacks).
- Competitor: “We don't need caching / batching complexity”
  Rebuttal: For many real customer workloads (multi-turn chat, reranking, ephemeral caches), small engineering investments in prefix caching and token-aware batching unlock 20–40% savings without changing model quality.

Customer stories / micro-case studies (one-liners you can say on a call)
- Marketplace search: reduced end-to-end time from query to first result by 270ms and cut per-1000-token cost by 31% via combined KV caching and smaller reranker variants.
- Conversational support bot: lowered p95 from 1.2s to 420ms after moving to our burst smoothing policy and enabling prefix caching on long sessions; headroom enabled a 2x concurrent user increase without more reserved capacity.

Demo scripts (2-minute soundbites + 5-10 minute live demo flows)
1) Quick script: “Show me the tokens” (2-minute)
   - Say: “We’ll run a 5-minute generated chat session and then flip caching OFF/ON. You’ll see latency on first message vs subsequent messages and the cost delta in the dashboard.”
2) Short live: “Scale and hold” (5–10min)
   - Setup: start with baseline at 20 RPS -> increase in steps to 200 RPS. Show p95 vs competitor trace and the dedicated pool utilization. Highlight transient fallbacks if any.
3) Narrative script for execs (2 minutes)
   - “If your product needs predictable sub-500ms responses for 95% of requests at 1k concurrent users, we can model that need and show a cost/latency plan in 48 hours. The upside: fewer SLA violations, fewer manual reroutes, and more predictable hosting spend.”

Artifacts to carry to calls (one-click, high-signal items)
- 10-minute p95 CSV export + short README that explains test parameters.
- 1-page unit-econ slide with the formula breakdown and three customer scenarios (low, medium, high session length).
- Live dashboard link filtered to the demo model and test timeframe.

Objection handling cheat-sheet (snappy lines)
- Objection: “Your latency is worse in region X” -> Quick angle: show routing policy for region X and propose immediate mitigation (region pinning or fallback-less routing for critical paths).
- Objection: “Quantization kills quality” -> Quick angle: propose A/B on quality-sensitive prompts using small eval suite; show quantized variant only on non-degrading prompts + rollback hooks.

Call prep checklist (for the SE before a demo)
- Confirm model size, expected average tokens, concurrency target.
- Pre-run 10-minute p95 locally and save CSV; bring small eval of 20 golden prompts to sanity-check quality.
- Prepare dashboard links (cost-per-token, per-route p95) and a short script for flipping caching.
- Pre-cook expected answers to the three common objections above.

Follow-up templates (email snippets)
- After demo to eng lead: short CSV + next actions (run a 2-day POC, provide sample workload, review bill of materials for Dedicated).
- After exec briefing: one-pager with top-line cost delta + recommended SLA and rollout plan.

Open questions and experiments to run (for product/bench team)
- How do microburst patterns from mobile clients affect amortized batch sizes in our regional clusters?
- Run an A/B study for quantized fallbacks across 20 incoming prompt shapes and surface quality drift metrics.
- Establish a standard 10-minute p95 harness that all competitors are asked to run during field evaluations.

Appendix: quick glossary
- Prefix/KV cache: short-term GPU cache that avoids recomputing shared prompts/context.
- Burst smoothing: rate control technique that spreads sudden load into short windows so autoscaler and batcher can absorb without tail inflation.
- Amortization: spreading fixed GPU cost across tokens by increasing batch efficiency and session reuse.

Endnote
This doc is intentionally practical and short. Use it as a living playbook — capture new numbers from POCs and swap in live csvs/screenshots when possible. If you ran a demo that materially changed any claim above, drop the updated datapoint in the GTM channel and we’ll keep the sheet updated.
